claims.text: Stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide formation in CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C is driven by controlled segregation of X to the alloy/oxide interface.
Segregation of X minimizes lattice mismatch at the alloy/oxide interface.
Segregation of X modifies alloy/oxide interfacial energy.
Reduced lattice mismatch and modified interfacial energy decelerate oxide growth.
Reduced lattice mismatch and modified interfacial energy reduce stress accumulation that would otherwise cause cracking or spallation.
The identity and concentration of X govern its segregation behavior and the resulting oxidation response.
In situ APT and TEM can be used to monitor interfacial segregation during oxidation.
A coherent oxide/metal interface is formed by segregated X.
X segregates to the alloy/oxide interface during high-temperature exposure.
Interfacial segregation of X suppresses the formation of interfacial stresses.
Suppressing interfacial stress prevents cracking and spallation of the oxide scale.
Compositions promoting favorable X segregation will form slow-growing, coherent oxide scales with minimal cracking.
Insufficient or improper X segregation will produce rapid oxide growth accompanied by cracking and spallation.
Lower or non-optimal X concentrations lack the required segregation and therefore produce unstable, defect-prone oxide scales.
The proposed mechanism applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys in oxidative or corrosive environments above 900 °C.
The proposed mechanism applies regardless of whether the alloy is a single-phase or multiphase solid solution.
The quantitative relationship among X segregation, lattice-mismatch reduction, and oxide stability remains unknown.
Failure of enhanced X segregation to reduce growth rate, improve coherence, and reduce cracking or spallation relative to baseline alloys would falsify the hypothesis.
